# Alfred North Whitehead Summary
Alfred North Whitehead was a philosopher whose work is characterized by his development of a process philosophy, a concept that posits that reality is composed of interrelated, dynamic events of "becoming" rather than static "being." He strongly rejected the notion of irreducible brute matter, viewing all things as experiential entities. His concept of perception, termed "prehension," describes how entities incorporate aspects of the perceived into themselves, distinguishing between causal efficacy and presentational immediacy. Furthermore, Whitehead's philosophy suggests that all things possess some measure of creativity or freedom, meaning nothing is entirely determined by mechanistic laws.
Whitehead's metaphysics informs his views on value and purpose; he posits that life is directed toward increasing its own satisfaction, which requires a goal. Regarding God, he criticized traditional monotheism for focusing too heavily on power, advocating instead for an idea of God as a "fellow-sufferer who understands." This conception of God involves a primordial nature (unlimited potentiality) and a consequent nature (receiving the world's activity). His philosophy has historically been influential in American progressive theology, and his ideas are also being applied to ecological civilization, sustainability, and educational reform.
